prompt.context: Your client is a large retail bank in the U.S. looking to move its current outsourced call center from India to Africa. The bank is currently evaluating 3 possible countries as a target location. The call center is focused on two types of calls: Customer Service Calls (account locked, password reset, etc.) and Sales Calls (pushing new services to new and existing clients, e.g. credit cards).
prompt.question: How would you evaluate each of these three African sites as a potential location for the new call center?

clarifying_info.q: Has the bank operated in Africa before?
clarifying_info.a: No. This is the bank's first time in Africa and it has no other current operations in the area.
Other competitors have already moved their call center operations to Africa.

exhibits.title: Typical Cost Structure for Call Center
exhibits.shows: A bar chart showing the percentage breakdown of a typical call center's cost structure across four cost categories plus a total bar.

exhibits.title: Call Demand Data by Country
exhibits.shows: A table comparing current India call center and three African countries (A, B, C) across utilization rate, labor rate, average call duration, and total working time. Also notes that the current call center has 400 employees and to assume 300 days/year for annual cost calculations.

framework: Financial: Focus on changes from current to future state — Operating costs (labor, rent, utilities, employee transport, overhead) and Investment costs (upfront capex that must be recoverable in a reasonable payback period)
Firm considerations: Alignment with firm strategy, lack of Africa experience, opportunity cost of capital
Market (Africa): Availability of English-speaking labor with banking knowledge, political stability, availability of infrastructure (internet, electricity, basic needs)
Competitive landscape: Have competitors already made this move successfully?
Risk to customers: Quality of service continuity

questions.prompt: What are some typical costs associated with running a call center, and which of these would be lower in Africa?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify that labor (40% of cost per Exhibit 1) is the key source of savings — all other costs (rent, utilities, misc.) are assumed to remain the same. Candidate should be pushed to isolate labor cost differences using utilization rate and headcount calculations. The current annual cost is $60M/year. Strong candidates note that new African call centers will initially be less effective (lower utilization) but should question rationale and push toward Exhibit 2.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, calculate the number of employees needed in each country to handle the same call volume as today, and determine the annual labor cost difference versus the current center.
questions.guidance: Candidate must use utilization rate to determine how many employees are needed to handle the same total calls. Current: 400 employees at 75% utilization produces 36K calls. Each country must also produce 36K calls. Labor cost is employee count x hourly rate x daily hours x 300 days. Strong candidates quickly note that Countries A and B have the same utilization (50%), so B is strictly better because its rate is $2/hr lower.

math.setup: Step 1 — Find total calls today: 400 employees x 75% utilization x 8 hrs/day x (1 call / 4 min) x 60 min/hr x 300 days. Simplify to find employees needed per country at their respective utilization rates then compute annual cost. Current labor cost = 400 x $25/hr x 8 hrs x 300 days = $24M/year (labor portion). Full center cost = $60M, labor = 40% = $24M confirms.
steps: Total calls produced per day: 400 employees x 75% x 8 hrs x (60/4 calls/hr) = 400 x 0.75 x 8 x 15 = 36,000 calls/day
Country A employees needed: 36,000 / (0.50 x 8 x 15) = 36,000 / 60 = 600 employees
Country B employees needed: same utilization as A = 600 employees
Country C employees needed: 36,000 / (0.25 x 8 x 15) = 36,000 / 30 = 1,200 employees
Annual labor cost — Current: 400 x $25 x 8 x 300 = $24,000,000
Annual labor cost — Country A: 600 x $10 x 8 x 300 = $14,400,000
Annual labor cost — Country B: 600 x $8 x 8 x 300 = $11,520,000
Annual labor cost — Country C: 1,200 x $6 x 8 x 300 = $17,280,000
Annual savings vs. current — Country A: $24M - $14.4M = $9.6M
Annual savings vs. current — Country B: $24M - $11.52M = $12.48M
Annual savings vs. current — Country C: $24M - $17.28M = $6.72M
Country B yields the greatest annual labor savings of $12.48M
math.answer: Country B saves $12.48M per year in labor costs, making it the most cost-effective option.

questions.prompt: If the investment required in each country is $36M, what is the payback period for Country B?
questions.guidance: Tests basic payback period concept. Strong candidates will mention a discount rate is theoretically needed but can proceed with simple payback for this exercise.

questions.prompt: Are there ways the call center can generate additional revenue?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm creative revenue streams from the physical facility and its captive population of employees.

brainstorming.prompt: Are there ways the Call Center can generate revenue?

categories.name: Family Services
ideas: Day care facilities for working parents

categories.name: Infrastructure Leverage
ideas: Internet café leveraging existing network infrastructure

categories.name: Facility Rental
ideas: Alternate use of facilities as a training center

categories.name: Advertising
ideas: Advertising revenue from posters and displays

recommendation: The client should move its call center to Country B, which is the most cost-effective option based on the combination of lower hourly labor rate ($8/hr vs. $10/hr for Country A) and equal productivity (50% utilization), yielding annual labor savings of $12.48M and a payback period of approximately 2.88 years on a $36M investment.
risks: Political instability in the region — security may be an added cost in some African countries (though told to include in investment)
Quality of service may decline, at least initially, given lower utilization rates and no prior Africa experience
No experience operating in Country B introduces execution and cultural risk
Long-term labor rate increases may erode savings as the market matures
Infrastructure costs (internet, electricity) may be higher than anticipated in Africa
next_steps: Work with local governments to gain support for the investment
Consider a pilot or phased approach to address service quality concerns during transition
Implement measures to increase employee utilization in Country B over time
Identify additional revenue opportunities and cost savings initiatives to hedge against future labor cost increases
Explore in-depth due diligence on Country B's political stability and infrastructure reliability
